articles.title: Startup Spotlight: An engineer’s search for better, safer baby products led him to launch Birch
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler
paras: A new baby can be the ultimate anxiety trigger: When will she sleep through the night? What if nursing is a challenge. What is that rash?! Given the countless unknowns, the last thing a parent needs are worries about the quality of the baby’s crib or the chemicals in a pacifier.
But when Karthik Gangiredla was preparing for the birth of his first daughter, he and his wife spent hours trying to figure out which baby products were trustworthy.
“We struggled a lot,” Gangiredla said. “We did a lot of research on what was safe, what’s not.”

An engineer with roughly 20 years of experience in supply chains and logistics, including roles at Amazon, Flexport and TikTok, Gangiredla found himself on the consumer side of the retail equation, scrutinizing strollers and bottles.

To spare other parents the same headache, he turned that research into Birch , an online marketplace that offers baby product buying guides and assigns each item a TrustScore. Its scoring system draws on certifications, lab reports and recall databases to help parents assess goods ranging from baby wipes to teething toys.
The site provides information on more than 10,000 items across 110 brands, including manufacturing locations, suppliers, certificate numbers and test reports.

Birch has contracts with brands it has checked out, and serves as their merchant of record, meaning if a customer has issues with a product or wants to return it, Birch handles those steps. It operates fulfillment centers in Los Angeles and New Jersey.
Gangiredla said the startup flips the e-commerce approach of retail giants, focusing on the shoppers’ needs, not those of the merchant. It does not accept ads or sponsored rankings.
If you took away the ad revenue for Amazon or TikTok, “the business wouldn’t exist,” Gangiredla said. “So it’s very difficult for them to approach the problem in a different way.”

The platform also offers a gift registry and tools for tracking fetal development during pregnancy, an infant’s nursing and sleep schedules, and other developmental steps. The tools are free for users.
We caught up with Gangiredla, Birch’s CEO and founder, for this edition of GeekWire’s Startup Spotlight.
In 50 words or less, give us your startup’s elevator pitch

Birch is the trust-first platform for baby and kids products and parenting resources. We research and score products across 50+ safety and quality signals before listing — and stock only what clears the bar — so parents skip the endless research and buy with confidence, from pregnancy through the toddler years.
What problem are you obsessed with solving?

The impossible research burden on new parents. Every purchase feels like a safety decision, the information is scattered and often unverified, and the stakes feel enormous. We’re obsessed with moving the work of figuring out what’s trustworthy off the parent and onto a system that does it rigorously — and then showing our work.
What surprised you after talking to customers?

How universal the trust problem is. We assumed it would track with income or with first-time parents, but our customers span all 50 states and every kind of household — big metros to small towns. And what they consistently want isn’t more options or a lower price; it’s someone to tell them, credibly, what’s actually worth buying.
How has AI changed the way you build your company?

It’s core, not a feature. Our TrustScore engine evaluates thousands of products across dozens of safety and quality signals in ways a human team our size never could, and the same intelligence powers discovery and personalization. It also lets a very lean team operate like a much larger one — and we now license that engine to other baby and kids brands as a product called Juno.
What’s one thing people misunderstand about your startup?

That “curated” means limited or expensive. Curation isn’t about carrying less for its own sake, or about selling premium — it’s about removing the untrustworthy. In our own data, price and trustworthiness barely correlate; some of the highest-scoring products are among the most affordable. Fewer and better, not fewer and pricier.
What’s the toughest decision you’ve made in the past year?

Turning away brands and revenue. When you’re early, every dollar is tempting — but our entire promise is that everything on Birch has earned its place. Saying no to products and partners that didn’t clear the bar, even when the revenue was real, was hard. It’s also the decision that defines what we are.
What’s the one piece of advice you give to other entrepreneurs?

Earn trust before you try to scale it. It’s slower and less glamorous than chasing growth, but trust compounds and shortcuts don’t. And talk to your customers far earlier, and far more often, than feels comfortable.
…a parent’s first instinct, the moment they find out they’re expecting, is to come to Birch — and “did you check the TrustScore?” is just how families talk about buying for their kids.

articles.title: How the surge in AI-discovered bugs is straining Microsoft security and threatening tech stability
articles.author: Angela Gunn
paras: It has come to the attention of the general public this month that adversaries successfully adopt technology a lot faster than defenders do. This has nothing to do with the willingness of defenders to try. It has everything to do with the ancient truth that to succeed, defenders have to get it right every time but adversaries only have to get it right occasionally.
Now multiply “every time” and “occasionally” by AI. Do you like that math? Does anyone?

The disastrous update that broke Teams, Outlook, SharePoint and other packages was not a direct attack by AI-wielding bad guys. Nor was the FAA outage . Nor were most of the outage events of the past few weeks, though who can say what’s up with those European Union refrigerators .

No. The true AI-driven mayhem has been predicated for several months now not on powerful new AI-honed attacks, but on an absolute deluge of bugs of relatively low severity that Microsoft and other defenders with a formal patch process aren’t built to process.

The question is whether traditional patch programs can adapt their processes to handle the deluge. Microsoft’s is MAPP (Microsoft Active Protections Program), to which the company has been committed for nearly two decades. If the industry-spanning events of the past few weeks are any indication, these programs can’t.

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said Wednesday at the New York Times DealBook Summit that last week’s Microsoft 365 outage came from a latent bug and wasn’t directly tied to AI, but he warned that AI-driven patching could bring more instability.
He elaborated in a separate appearance on CNBC the same day, saying the flood of patches being applied to older infrastructure is making systems less stable.

AI has “allowed us to find these bugs and fix these bugs, but that means you’ve got to then patch them, and that creates instability,” Nadella said, when asked by Jim Cramer about a string of recent outages at United, Schwab, Chase and other organizations.

Some context: MAPP turned 18 this year. The program, run by the MSRC (Microsoft Security Response Center), handles outreach to partner companies that gain early access to information on the bugs in advance of each month’s Patch Tuesday release. In-house, it coordinates the patch release process, just as the larger MSRC organization helps coordinate the handling of bug reports from external finders.

MSRC also runs point on prioritizing patches of the worst bugs through its SSIRP (Software and Services Incident Response Plan) program, itself dating to 2004. In its time, it was an industry leader in how companies can efficiently get their arms around bad bugs.

MAPP in its own way is similarly remarkable. It has undergone a few traumas over the years, usually when a partner breaks confidence and leaks the advance details it receives. In 2025, after attacks on SharePoint raised suspicions of a leak from the program, Microsoft stopped giving Chinese companies early access . But MAPP continues to tick along in a way that would make any program manager proud. Other companies have their own version of MAPP / MSRC, as do community efforts such as those supporting Linux.

Full disclosure: I’m a former MSRC employee who learned about MAPP at the knee of the program’s principals. I subsequently tracked patch releases at a company partnered with MAPP at its highest (Validate) level, which means I was privy to the 14-day multi-stage run-up to each month’s release. I admire and respect the program… and I’m afraid that in the AI-finder era, it’s in big, big trouble.

Since January 2021, Microsoft has issued patches for an estimated 10,319 CVEs. (I use estimated numbers throughout this analysis because there are various ways of counting such things, including whether or not the patch accrues to an application such as Edge, which actually relies on the Chromium project for its fixes. Other analysts arrive at larger or smaller counts.)
Over half of those — 5,383 CVEs — are 2026 releases, 5,128 of which were addressed since April. In comparison, 2025’s full-year CVE total was 1,180.
What happened in April? As nearly as analysis can determine, the floodgates opened and finders (security researchers) started barraging the company with reports.

The first quarter of 2026 saw 255 CVEs addressed over three months. April had 163, May 132; in June the number jumped to 209. In July it was off to the races with 575 CVEs. In October, the monthly count topped 1,400.

Most of these bugs aren’t coming from the usual security stalwarts. They’re coming from new finders, they’re coming in with multiple simultaneous finders not believed to be working together, and they’re coming in relatively weak.
Though the overall volume has skyrocketed, the number per month of bugs under active exploit in the wild — the notorious “zero-days” — hasn’t increased proportionally.

Moreover, average bug severity has in fact decreased. Until 2026, the average CVSS severity score for all bugs tended to hover around 7.8 (out of 10) each month. In 2026, that’s dropped to approximately 7.4 as of September — not garbage finds, but the sort of thing that doesn’t scramble the jets.
No surge in zero-days and a drop in severity — that’s good news. The problem is the volume.
Once bugs are received by Microsoft, each goes through a MAPP-helmed, multi-team process of investigation and patch development.

Since many products have several versions still in support, that often means that multiple teams within each product group are asked to ingest a bug report, replicate the problem, devise and test a fix, ensure the fix doesn’t trigger other problems or inadvertently point to a similar bug elsewhere in the product and ready it for mass consumption. Even AI slop has to be taken seriously, just in case.

Meanwhile, MAPP is the traffic cop for the entire release, working with each team to ascertain patches are ready, understand the nature of the bugs and what can be safely communicated to partners and the public, and ready the processes that make the second Tuesday of each month a festival of downloads and reboots. From where we stand right now, it’s all fairly… hand-crafted.

In theory the process is automatable to some extent, though the success of that effort so far in light of recent events is debatable. But high volume also leads to other problems, such as exposing information on incomplete patching.
For instance, Microsoft has recently patched Office bugs that apply to both Windows and Mac, but patches have initially only been available for Windows versions.

Microsoft’s release-day information about such bugs — patching Windows versions while asking Apple users to monitor Microsoft communications for news of their own patch — alerts the world, including eager adversaries, that the flaw exists. Apple customers just have to hope no adversaries exploit it while their patch is pending.

More broadly, many of the steps in the current patching process involve judgment calls, not processes that scale well or that can reliably be handled by existing AI-driven systems. In Microsoft’s case, MAPP is a remarkably small team of humans and, being security folk at Microsoft, they’re not always the loudest or most popular voice in Redmond.

Add the mercurial nature of finders, who may or may not provide full details on their bugs (ask any MSRC person how often they receive a crash dump and a demand for payment) and may or may not disclose their finds publicly if they don’t feel they’re getting sufficient response.

Do not add the kind of defender staffing needed to handle a massive increase in volume — either in MAPP or in the individual product groups building the actual patches — because in the AI era, it’s likely the companies won’t add it either.
The cracks are showing. Microsoft has been compelled to issue OOB (out-of-band) releases and servicing updates monthly since July, often within just a few days of the original release.

OOBs are important enough to merit release outside the usual patch cadence, often because there’s a security issue involved, but they’re tough on administrators already wading through a slew of regularly scheduled patching. With volumes high, patch testers may rush or elide certain steps, such as checking that a fix doesn’t break something deeper in the system.

Nadella told the DealBook audience this week that a patch for a critical bank system might once have been tested for a week. Now, he said, the patch “needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production because it’s being exploited in the wild. So that’s going to create instability.”

Think of MAPP as Mariners catcher Dan Wilson in 2001: a pro handling a staff of skilled human pitchers, one pitch at a time. Now it’s 2026, and the pitchers have been swapped for a bank of mediocre pitching machines all slinging fastballs at … 2026-era Dan Wilson.

Here, again, AI can’t fix a system that requires defenders to catch every pitch. Secondary lines of defense that have worked in the past — for instance, the requirement by various regulatory programs that enterprises ascertain that patches are safe for their own systems — rely heavily on companies sending out the soundest possible patches.

Managed service providers might at least make sure that patches are flagged to customers as available, relevant and urgent. But they’re in no position to do much more than trust that what’s shipped is safe to deploy and react when things go wrong.
Even that gets harder when a bug kneecaps the security tools they depend on. Last week’s Microsoft 365 outage affected parts of Microsoft Defender that interact with Exchange Online.

It’s not just Microsoft, of course. The Linux community is seriously suffering , and both Apple and (especially) Google have struggled with patch-release quality in 2026 as evidenced by their own emergency updates and post-release device instability reports. Industry-wide, ecosystems built around reliable, transparent patch cadences and patch-development processes have never seemed more in danger of being overwhelmed.

What needs to happen? Sure, build those AI systems; the marketing people will be pleased. It’ll speed up some parts of the process. But a system capable of replicating, every time, the human judgment calls that go into the patch-release process isn’t going to magically create itself; people have to create it.
Is there some chance that the deluge will ebb — that researchers and their tools will at some point finally find all the bugs in all the world’s products?

It’s a pretty thought, and some relief may eventually come. When more and more unrelated finders turn up the same bug, it gives one hope that the set is finite. But no one knows when relief will come, and most folk in tech suspect that really, no, there is no bottom to the bug barrel. Nor, for the foreseeable future, any rest for the weary.

articles.title: StepSecurity, led by two Microsoft vets, raises $20M to defend developers’ tools from hackers
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: StepSecurity’s co-founders spent more than two decades combined at Microsoft. This week, as their startup announced a new round of funding , its researchers were also investigating a hacked Microsoft software package .
Their old employer is not the only one with this problem.

StepSecurity , a Seattle-area cybersecurity startup, raised a $20 million Series A round led by Elephant, with participation from existing investors Runtime Ventures, Inner Loop Capital and SaaS Ventures. The company has now raised $23 million, including a $3 million seed round in 2024 . Axios Pro first reported the latest round .
The startup protects the systems used to build software: developers’ laptops, code repositories, package downloads and CI/CD pipelines, the automated systems that assemble and ship code.

The problem is that attackers increasingly slip malicious code into open-source software that developers download. That code can do damage as soon as it runs on a developer’s laptop or build system, stealing the passwords and keys that unlock other systems.
“A supply chain attack used to take a skilled team,” CEO Varun Sharma wrote in a blog post announcing the funding . “Now one person can vibe code it.”

Sharma spent about 15 years at Microsoft, where he led a team in Azure Security focused on making security easier for developers. CTO Ashish Kurmi spent nearly eight years at Microsoft before leading cloud security at Uber and infrastructure security at Plaid.
The two met at Microsoft and started StepSecurity in 2021, after working through the fallout from the SolarWinds and Codecov supply chain attacks at their respective employers.
A busy week: The Microsoft package, agent-framework, is the Python version of Microsoft’s open-source toolkit for building AI agents.

It gets roughly 190,000 downloads a month. Two malicious versions published on Nov. 17 to PyPI, the main public repository for Python software, included code designed to steal cloud and CI/CD credentials as soon as Python started up, SecurityWeek reported . PyPI quarantined both versions, and a Microsoft maintainer said an investigation was underway.

That’s one entry in a long list. StepSecurity’s announcement also cites the $6.3 billion Binance breach in October, which the FBI attributed to North Korea’s TraderTraitor group. Binance has said the attack started with a compromised employee laptop.

It also points to a tampered copy of Anthropic’s Claude Code extension that sat in Cursor’s extension marketplace for about 11 hours last month. Cursor said up to 5,000 users may have received the malicious version.

StepSecurity says it documented 56 confirmed compromises of trusted software components between August 2025 and August 2026, and roughly one every three days from March 2026 through the August report.

How it works: StepSecurity got its start with its own tool, Harden-Runner, which is free for open-source projects. It watches automated builds on GitHub and flags anything unexpected in the processes they run, the network connections they make or the files they change.

More than 20,000 open-source projects use it, the company says, up from about 3,000 at the time of the seed round. Unusual behavior spotted in those public builds has helped StepSecurity catch attacks early, the company says, including the March 2025 compromise of tj-actions, a widely used add-on for GitHub’s build automation.

StepSecurity’s paid products also protect developers’ laptops and check code repositories. Its Secure Registry service screens software packages before a company’s builds download them from public sources such as npm, the main public repository for JavaScript packages. It blocks versions known to be compromised and holds brand-new releases for a waiting period, giving researchers time to catch malicious ones before anyone installs them.

Along with the funding, StepSecurity is making Secure Registry free for public GitHub projects that use Harden-Runner and run their builds on GitHub’s servers. The free version defaults to a two-day waiting period and supports JavaScript packages, with Python, Java, Ruby and Rust planned.

StepSecurity has plenty of competition. Socket, a San Francisco startup that screens open-source packages for malicious code, raised $60 million at a $1 billion valuation in May. Sonatype, JFrog and Endor Labs also sell tools that can block risky packages before they’re installed.
Growth spurt: StepSecurity says its annual recurring revenue grew fivefold in 2024, fivefold again in 2025 and more than fivefold so far this year. It didn’t disclose dollar figures.
Named customers include Circle, Dexcom, Kong, Mercari, Chainguard and XBOW.

The company has 27 employees, up from four, including the founders, at the time of the seed round. Sharma is based in Sammamish and Kurmi in Kirkland, and the rest of the remote-first team is spread across the U.S., Canada and India.

What’s next: StepSecurity plans to extend its protections to agent sandboxes, the isolated environments where AI agents run code. Its argument is that anyone who asks an AI agent for a spreadsheet may be downloading and running open-source packages.
The company says it also plans to double its team over the next 12 months, mostly in security research, engineering and sales and marketing.

articles.title: John Deere acquires Orchard Robotics, an AI farming startup with Seattle ties
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler
paras: Orchard Robotics , an agtech company using artificial intelligence to help growers monitor crops and make farming decisions, has been acquired by John Deere. The deal was announced Thursday and the terms were not disclosed.

The startup has developed a system of cameras mounted on tractors and other equipment that gather images as the machines traverse a farm. Orchard’s AI analyzes the images to generate data on vines, trees and crops, which is then used to track growth, yield and health.

“This acquisition connects crop-level intelligence with John Deere technology and equipment that can precisely execute the work in the field,” Tim Marquis, John Deere’s director of farm systems innovation, said in a statement.
That includes helping farmers target treatments and make better-timed decisions about thinning, spraying and harvesting.
Orchard was founded by CEO Charlie Wu , a Thiel Fellow who dropped out of Cornell University to launch his business in 2022.

“Over these next few years, our goal is to bring the power of Orchard’s industry-leading technology and AI Farming capabilities to every farmer out there,” Wu said in a LinkedIn post . “This is only the beginning of a long and awesome journey ahead.”
The startup is based in San Francisco and has an office in Seattle. Wu splits his time between the two cities and was a finalist for Young Entrepreneur of the Year at the 2026 GeekWire Awards.
Orchard has raised more than $25 million from investors, including a $22 million Series A round announced in September 2025. The startup has 45 employees, according to PitchBook.

The Pacific Northwest is home to numerous agtech startups. That includes other companies that collect and analyze data, such as Loftus Labs and innov8.ag, as well as IUNU and Koidra, which are focused on greenhouse crops. Businesses tackling field operations include weed destroyers Carbon Robotics and Aigen; rock-removing TerraClear; and irrigation startups FarmHQ and Verdi.

articles.title: RBC Signals brings in $10M investment to expand strategic frontiers for satellite services
articles.author: Alan Boyle
paras: Redmond, Wash.-based RBC Signals has announced a $10 million strategic growth investment aimed at accelerating the company’s expansion into government satellite data services and the commercialization of emerging space technologies.
RBC Signals supports satellite operators by arranging access to a global network of ground stations, including its own assets and antenna facilities operated by partners.

In August, for example, Blue Origin and RBC Signals announced a partnership to build out the ground infrastructure for Blue Origin’s Quartz communications network. RBC Signals is also a provider for the U.S. Space Force’s Joint Antenna Marketplace .

The newly announced investment was led by Washington Harbour Partners , a private investment firm based in Washington, D.C. The firm ranked sixth among all defense technology investors in the Silicon Valley Defense Group’s 2026 NatSec100 Report .

“Our vision has always been to build a global, secure network of networks that makes space connectivity more accessible, flexible and reliable,” Ron Faith, RBC Signals’ president and CEO, said today in a news release .

“By bringing together infrastructure, partners and emerging technologies, we’re creating a dual-use platform that can evolve alongside the needs of the national defense and the commercial space industry,” Faith said. “This investment from Washington Harbour Partners will help us accelerate that vision by expanding our government services business and bringing emerging capabilities such as higher frequency bands, optical connectivity, intersatellite links and space domain awareness to market.”

Mina Faltas, founder and CEO of Washington Harbour Partners, highlighted RBC Signals’ role in addressing the growing demand for space connectivity. “We see tremendous potential in the company’s ability to deliver mission-critical capabilities, and we’re excited to support the team as they enter this next phase of growth,” Faltas said.

articles.title: Jackson Street Housing Project Could Leave King County on Hook for Millions
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: A proposal from King County Executive Girmay Zahilay to finance an affordable housing project is raising some eyebrows at the County Council, due to a draft lease agreement that could leave the County's general fund on the hook for unexpected cost increases for years down the line. The project, at 701 S Jackson Street in Seattle's Chinatown-International District (CID), would include 111 new, mostly family-sized units along with retail space but also turn King County into a tenant charged with paying off bonds used for building construction.

The ordinance currently in front of the County Council would provide financing to a $63.8 million apartment building that has been stalled for many years. Developers Nitze-Stagen and the Housing Diversity Corporation, operating as a joint entity called O.Z. Navigator, secured permits for 701 S Jackson Street in 2022 as a 238-unit building, mostly one-bedroom units and studios.

Going in on a site previously owned by the CID's storied Mar family, the former gas station required significant site remediation work to make it suitable for housing. And even though that remediation work is now complete, the construction project was never able to move forward due to financing issues.

Six years later, the project has been redesigned with far more family-sized units, making it more attractive to public financers following an oversaturation of Seattle's studio and one-bedroom affordable housing market. Of 111 total apartments, 96 would be two-bedrooms, and 14 would be three-bedroom, all available to residents making 67% of King County's area median income or below – around $90,000 per year for a family of three. Designs include one one-bedroom unit.

Included in a slate of housing investments tucked into Zahilay's proposed mid-biennial budget update this fall, the 701 S Jackson project was notable in that it was missing a specific dollar commitment, in contrast with line items like a $4 million earmark for the Pacific Tower Quarters Building in Beacon Hill and $1.8 million for a veteran's housing project in Kirkland.
That's because the deal in the International District would be structured very differently than the other projects.

Under the ordinance that could be voted on as soon as December 8, King County would serve as the third party on a Development Services Agreement with the Housing Diversity Corporation and a nonprofit specifically set up for the project, 701 Essential Housing. That entity would issue up to $90 million in tax-exempt bonds to build the project, with Housing Diversity Corporation the developer.

"Upon completion of construction, the Master Lease Agreement would be effective, allowing the County to lease the property from 701 Essential Housing," a staff report from late October noted. "On behalf of the County, 701 Essential Housing would manage subleases for residential and retail tenants. The County would make payments to 701 Essential Housing to cover any remaining debt service and operations costs not covered by sublease revenue. At the end of the 30-year lease term and full repayment of the bonds, the County would assume ownership of the property."

In the financial scenario envisioned by Zahilay's office, the County would be responsible for paying $37.5 million over the life of the project, with a maximum annual payment of around $2.5 million in 2032 that ramps down over time.

King County Chief Budget Officer Aaron Rubardt told councilmembers that the County's general fund, under significant strain in recent years by restrictions on property tax growth and limited growth in unincorporated areas outside cities, is currently tabbed as the primary source of revenue for the project. But Rubardt also noted that another funding source could be found at a later time – potentially the countywide housing levy that Zahilay has been formally considering since shortly after taking office.

"The proposal is for the general fund to back this, and we built into our general fund projections that the general fund would pay the debt service," Rubardt told councilmembers. "But over time, the Executive and Council can make a decision to have another funding source fund it. So I think that is fungible over time. So keep that in mind, it doesn't all have to be paid by the general fund, but the obligation that we're signing up for does obligate the general fund as the backer of the debt."

A $37.5 million general fund contribution to fund 111 units would amount to one of the largest set-asides for an individual affordable housing project in King County history. The proposed investment works out to just over $337,000 per unit, albeit spaced out over 30 years.

In 2025, King County’s Housing Finance Program awarded $23.7 million to eight projects total, helping to advance a collective total of 672 homes – however, all of those projects were receiving additional financing on top of any County contribution.

But as laid out in staff analysis presented during Tuesday's work session, the county's contribution isn't fixed in place. Various scenarios could play out that would balloon that number, including lower-than-expected occupancy of the rental units, increased construction costs, and higher interest rates.

With a 30% increase in project costs, the staff presentation noted, the County contribution could end up at $77.2 million, doubling the amount in projected pro-forma plan that the Zahilay administration presented. With a 1% more expensive bond coupon, costs could go up by $20 million. A vacancy rate at 701 S Jackson Street that is double what's currently expected could cost the County an additional $13 million, despite the fact that the County would not be in control of managing the rentals itself.
Even more worrying for the general fund is the fact that these scenarios could all occur to various degrees, with nothing constraining the top cost that the County would be held responsible for.
"It is not possible to predict which of these scenarios, or which combination, might occur," this week's updated staff report noted.

During the meeting, Rubardt faced questions about why the deal was structured in this specific way, with Rubardt pointing to the need to stand up affordable units quickly. A slowdown in development traced to higher interest rates and higher operating costs for existing affordable housing buildings does mean that there are fewer shovel-ready projects that the County could plug itself into.

"The priority was for 111 family-sized units in the International District, two bedrooms and three bedrooms," Rubardt said. "The reason we are proposing this now under this arrangement is that we think it's a fast way, a relatively fast way, to get something built and to open up those affordable housing units, so we can have them open in 2029, hopefully."
Executive's Office spokesperson Callie Craighead provided additional information about Zahilay's decision to turn to this type of lease agreement in a follow-up email to The Urbanist .

"This is a new financing model for the County for funding affordable housing; however, it is not new to the county," Craighead wrote. "King County has used this financing model for other buildings, including office buildings in the downtown office core. This financing model has also been used by local universities to fund dormitories. The County is looking for innovative ways to finance urgent housing needs. "

"This funding arrangement provided the flexibility to fund affordable housing relatively quickly; and at the end of agreement the County will have acquired both the land and facility," Craighead added.

In the rosy scenario, that transfer could provide the County an asset that could operate at a profit, generating a revenue stream for additional public investments in housing or otherwise. In the not-so-rosy scenario, the County could inherit an aging building with a maintenance backlog for which it would continue to be on the hook.

Though Zahilay's office is pushing for a vote on the agreement before the end of 2026, Tuesday's meeting was the first substantive conversation to occur on the proposal at the council level – an October 28 briefing was cancelled due to other agenda items running long.
During the recent work session, several councilmembers raised clear concerns about exposing the general fund to this level of unexpected cost increases.

"I think I heard that it would be difficult for us to legislate to share that risk differently," Councilmember Claudia Balducci said. "Although I would recommend that we try, because you know, if we're taking all of the risk, that's a tough ask for the County's general fund."
Craighead defended Zahilay's approach to managing King County's finances.

"The Executive always scrutinizes allocating limited General Fund dollars and limiting the fiscal risk to the County," Craighead wrote. "As part of his commitment to building a better government, Executive Zahilay’s proposed second omnibus budget maintains the General Fund’s emergency reserves at 8% and the 'rainy day fund.' The Executive and the Budget Team is starting to work through scenario planning for the 2028-2029 budget to minimize risk and deliver a balanced budget."

Following the work session, the council held a closed-door discussion of the legal risks behind the deal, a session held at the request of Councilmember Jorge Barón. If the ordinance is rejected, that would represent the biggest break between Zahilay's office and the County Council so far during his term, with the council largely deferring to Executive branch priorities so far.
On the other hand, it's possible that the council is able to come around to Zahilay's proposal, potentially by putting additional guardrails on the lease agreement.
Balducci noted that if the general fund ends up getting tapped more than expected to meet the County's obligations, that could lead to service cuts elsewhere in County government.
"People lose their jobs, and we end up cutting vital services," Balducci said. "So, I just think we need to be very clear about what risk we're taking on and how good or bad we feel about that."

articles.title: Tacoma Council Axes Crisis Response Team, Slashes City Budget to Address Deficit
articles.author: Carolyn Bick
paras: Facing a major fiscal cliff to the tune of $40 million over the next biennium, the City of Tacoma was forced to make sharp cuts to its 2027-2028 biennial budget, which the Tacoma City Council adopted in a unanimous vote Tuesday.

These cuts included eliminating more than 100 staff positions, 14 of which were filled, as well as cutting the City’s fairly new civilian co-responder Holistic Outreach Promoting Engagement (HOPE) team, and whittling down the police department’s community service officer (CSO) team.

Even though these cost-saving measures reduced the City’s 2027-2028 deficit back down to zero, this doesn’t mean that Tacoma is in the clear for the long term. The City still projects an $18 million budget shortfall by the time the next biennial budget rolls around. By the 2031-2032 biennium, the City will once again face a $40 million shortfall.

Public reaction to the decision to cut the HOPE Team, a program through the Tacoma Fire Department, was especially negative. Several members of the public, including a number of community activists and a representative from the NAACP, called for its retention and for the City to revisit how it dispatched the team. At least one member of the public said that they felt like the city was breaking the promise it had made in the wake of Manuel Ellis’s death in custody of Tacoma police officers in March 2020.

But civilian crisis response is not permanently off the table. The City introduced two amendments that put $150,000 towards a crisis response study and $400,000 toward crisis response and case management support. The latter amendment is meant as a bridge to sustain some capacity for crisis response between HOPE’s elimination and whatever team may replace it. The HOPE team had been budgeted at $4 million over the next two years before the cuts.

The city will also retain five of the 10 total community service officer positions through the Tacoma Police Department. These officers handle non-emergency calls. The City had initially considered entirely eliminating this cohort of officers.
“For years,” a slide in the city’s Oct. 27 budget presentation reads, “the cost of running the City has grown almost twice as fast as the money it collects.”

At that meeting — which served as the first hearing for the proposed biennial budget — the City’s finance director, Andy Cherullo, told councilmembers that the City had been facing a $40 million structural deficit in the General Fund. Without the proposed cuts, he continued, the structural deficit would grow to $75 million by the 2029-2030 biennium, and $106 million by the 2031-2032 biennium.
But this doesn’t mean the City is out of the woods.
“We are still projecting structural deficits in the next couple of biennium,” Cherullo said. “There are further hard decisions in the future for this City Council.”
The impending budget shortfall isn’t for lack of trying — and it isn’t an unfamiliar problem.
State law limits how quickly some revenues can grow. For instance, property tax levies can only grow at a rate of 1% per year.

“There’s no City expense that grows at 1% per year,” Cherullo said. “Just like our community members, the City is not immune to the higher inflation currently in the economy. We are also facing higher costs for fuel, supplies, and services. Benefits like health care are growing at double-digit rates, and there's general uncertainty related to what direction the overall economy will move that can impact other City revenues like sales tax and our business and occupation taxes.”
There is also an increasing demand for City services, and wages, benefits, and supplies cost more every year.
Together, this all creates a difficult situation for the City.

“Unless the state gives us more opportunities to have progressive revenue sources at the local level, we’re going to continue to have these problems year after year after year, and it’s been happening for the last 24 years,” Deputy Mayor Joe Bushnell said at the council’s Nov. 10 meeting. “So people are wondering, ‘Well why can’t the City be creative about these different things?’ It’s because we are struggling to fund basic services as it is. We can’t be as creative as we’d like to be because we don’t have the revenue sources or the options available to us from beyond our powers here.”
In passing the budget, Bushnell was also the only member of the council to acknowledge that the City had cut staffed positions.

“I […] want to recognize that through this budget, we eliminated 100 positions, and behind many of those positions were people, great dedicated staff doing amazing work on behalf of our community,” he said at the Nov. 17 meeting. “A hundred positions have been eliminated out of this budget, and I just don’t want us to lose sight of that fact, because that’s not actually a good thing, I think, for our city, because those are services that are not going to be rendered.”

City Manager Hyun Kim told The Urbanist in a later interview that cutting the 14 filled positions was not an easy decision, and that the City’s Human Resources worked hard to identify where it could keep staff whose positions were originally going to be cut. Prior to budget deliberations, a little more than half of identified positions were filled.

“[W]e got that number down to 14. […] We really did try our best to give as much advance notice to our employees that are impacted employees in those filled positions and that's why we gave the notice, we gave options,” Kim said. “We were not completely successful because as was mentioned last night by our deputy mayor, there's a human story here. We've got 14 individuals that will receive layoff notices in the coming days. It's one of the hardest things that I have to do in this job.”

In a later interview, Mayor Anders Ibsen told The Urbanist that, for the last several months, he has been having discussions with lawmakers and leaders from other jurisdictions about new legislation that could allow jurisdictions to find new sources of revenue and break out of the restrictive revenue-sourcing cycle that repeatedly forces them into difficult budget cycles.

Ibsen said that the state may be facing severe budget challenges, but that isn’t just due to the economy. It’s also because of the state’s limited tax code. In many ways, he said, that sets local communities up to fail “because we have revenue sources that are always going to decline relative to inflation. That's why we're always in cut situations. That's not sustainable or fair, and it needs to change.”

“What you're going to see cities like Tacoma push for in the legislative session […] as the legislature approaches the tax code, is to make sure we don't have a two-tiered system where the state passes unfunded mandates down to us [which] gives us local taxing options,” Ibsen said. “We don't want to just continue having local taxing options. We want to have tools, but we also want to make sure that we have a unified tax code that is a shared burden for funding core services like public education, public safety, homelessness, you name it. It has to be a shared approach rather than robbing Peter to pay Paul.”
The city initially created the five-person HOPE Team three years ago, following the 2020 Black Lives Matter protests and the death of Manuel Ellis in Tacoma police custody in 2020.

In justifying cutting the team, the City appeared to suggest that the HOPE Team had been underutilized in its three years in existence. A slide from the council’s Oct. 27 meeting states that the HOPE Team answered about three calls per day in 2026, that it was hard to staff, and that the team was only available for limited hours. City policy also requires police officers or firefighters on the scene for safety reasons.
The Tacoma Fire Department also initially put out an Oct. 27 joint press release with the Tacoma Police Department explaining the pending cuts of the HOPE and CSO teams.

Though both departments pulled the press release shortly after its publication, the departments stated in that press release that both teams had “struggled to maintain intended staffing levels and have never been adequately positioned to effectively serve the community” from the get-go. The departments said that the teams responded to just a “fraction” of service calls the department received.

“One of the primary goals of HOPE was to relieve traditional first responders to focus their duty on calls where behavioral health issues were not the primary need for service,” the joint press release stated. “In many cases, HOPE and CSO efforts have proven redundant. Nearly all HOPE responses, for example, have also required the presence of paramedics, police officers, or firefighters. In reality, 99% of HOPE requests have required traditional first responder co-response since July 2023.”

But several members of the public argued that the HOPE Team — at barely three years old, with no studies showing its efficacy or lack thereof — was hardly getting a fair hearing, and that the City was cutting it prematurely.

“It’s accurate when everybody says that HOPE has been underfunded, understaffed, and underutilized, and I want to tell you that that is, in fact, your fault,” said Jonathan Pottle at the council’s Oct. 27 meeting. “Axing the HOPE Team is not an operational necessity. It’s an ideological choice, and it is a bad one.”

Both Theresa Power-Drutis, a longtime community organizer who works as the director of the New Connections re-entry program, and Barb Church, an environmental and community activist, told councilmembers that they needed to reconsider the way the HOPE Team is dispatched and accessible, rather than just eliminate it.

“If the team is eliminated, what happens? Police or fire will transport those in crisis to emergency rooms or shelters or jail. … However, shelters, jails, and emergency rooms do not provide resources for long-term mental health recovery,” added Calista Brown, another member of the public.

Like Power-Drutis and Church, Brown also suggested that the city “consider creative ways to enable HOPE’s operating at the capacity that truly meets community needs” and “how to offset ongoing understaffing, how to institute independent deployment.” She also highlighted that “police and fire have required co-response shutting down direct community access.”
“Review all the data that HOPE has collected so that the how and why of HOPE's effectiveness informs your decision to keep, eliminate, or truncate it,” Brown said.

“We have heard police officers say repeatedly that they are not trained to respond to mental health crises. […] A number of Tacoma police officers have described the HOPE Team as beneficial and stated they would like to see the HOPE Team expanded into late-night hours to be able to provide more extended support,” said Julie Andrzejewski, the co-chair of Indivisible Tacoma. “It's a cost-effective service. Eliminating it will result in greater costs, both human and financial.”

Gemini, a member of Tacoma Alliance Against Racist and Political Repression, seconded several other pro-HOPE commenters, and likewise underscored that the team didn’t even get a fighting chance. They also reminded the city of the financial cost of having no crisis responders.

“It’s kind of callous to talk about saving people's lives in the measure of dollars, but I understand we’re talking about a budget,” Gemini said. “I think we really need to think about how much money is spent when the police are dispatched to these crises. How much money was spent when SWAT was sent to Rhoda Butler’s house and shot her down and killed her? How much did that cost the city? How much did it cost the city to defend Manny Ellis’s murderers and pay out those murderers for the tunes of millions of dollars? […] We need to be weighing the real cost of police violence and [ … ] institutional violence against how much the HOPE Team costs, even if it was fully funded.”

During public comment at the council’s Nov. 10 meeting, Tacoma community member Nikki SnowKing member of the public who identified herself as Nikki reminded the council that it had made “an explicit promise to this community in the wake of Black Lives Matter and a call for accountability.”

“We were promised that Tacoma would fundamentally change its approach to public safety. You promised to invest in human-centered, non-police responses that protect rather than endanger our most vulnerable community members,” Nikki said. “The HOPE program is a direct realization of these promises. […] Dismantling the program is a clear retreat from the commitments that were made in Manuel Ellis’ name and to the Black and vulnerable communities of Tacoma.”

Ibsen told The Urbanist that “the promise that the city made was to keep Tacoma safe, while also partnering with the community to build on that trust, and the key behind that isn't the programs, it's the essence of what we're doing.”

articles.title: Friday Roundtable: Sound Transit Bingo
articles.author: Michael Smith
paras: To celebrate 30 years since voters passed Sound Move , Sound Transit is hosting a transit Bingo game today. Sound Move was the Central Puget Sound Regional Transit Authority’s first voter approved funding package to build a regional transit system. The Sound Transit brand was not adopted until 1997. Sound Move included commuter rail between Everett-Seattle and Lakewood-Seattle, light rail in Tacoma and between Seattle-SeaTac, and an extensive network of express buses in Snohomish, King, and Pierce counties.

The first component of Sound Move to enter service, ST Express, began on September 19, 1999 with nine routes. Commuter rail service started the following year with trips between Seattle and Tacoma. The agency’s first light rail line, then-called Tacoma Link, opened in August 2003. Light rail service in Seattle, Central Link, began service on July 18, 2009 between downtown Seattle and Tukwila.

Everyone is invited to explore the region while visiting stations to fill in their Bingo card today between 10am to 2pm. The first 450 people to complete a row, column, or diagonal and return their card to a designated drop-off will get a 30th Anniversary ORCA card . Everyone who gets Bingo will be entered into a raffle to win additional prizes. If you want to go above and beyond, complete every square for a chance to win a grand prize that includes one year of free transit and a behind-the-scenes ride-along through a Link train wash. For more details and the complete list of prizes, visit the Sound Transit website .

articles.title: Thanks to new generation of office space, Capitol Hill’s daytime population ranges from Duolingo to start-ups
articles.author: CHS
paras: CENTRL Office’s Capitol Hill Location (Image: Matt Freire)
Building out a traditional office on Capitol Hill comes with real overhead — even for small upgrades.

According to City of Seattle construction permits signed off this month, language-learning giant Duolingo spent a base $18,000 on interior alterations just to add a dedicated lactation room inside its fifth-floor offices inside the net-zero energy Bullitt Center at 15th and Madison

While established companies can absorb bespoke buildouts and permitting timelines, Capitol Hill’s smaller office rentals and coworking spaces are giving homegrown entrepreneurs an affordable alternative, offering shared amenities and flexible footprints without the upfront capital expense.

As remote and hybrid work spaces reshape how businesses utilize office space, coworking and office rentals are seeing an increased interest from freelancers and small teams, according to the developers behind the spaces.

While overall Seattle office vacancy remained elevated at 27.7% in Q3 2026, it has begun edging down from its peak and neighborhood submarkets are faring substantially better than the downtown core, according to commercial real estate firm Kidder Mathews . In the Capitol Hill and Central District submarket, total vacancy stood at 10.5% across 4.8 million square feet of inventory, compared to 35% downtown. Locally, Capitol Hill’s CENTRL Office reported a 30% increase in occupancy over the past year.
Kaitee Quinn , general manager at CENTRL, said that these environments are becoming an essential stepping stone in business growth today.

“I think we’re filling a need that has been created by everybody preferring remote and hybrid work now,” Quinn said. “You get to choose to come to a space that’s beautiful, that’s lively, and meet people in your neighborhood.”

Duolingo’s own Capitol Hill footprint followed that trajectory. Before signing its direct lease at the Bullitt Center, the company’s Seattle team operated out of coworking desks inside the historic Kelly-Springfield building on 11th Ave — the same space CENTRL Office now operates.

As regulatory and operating costs rise across the city, these smaller office rentals and coworking spaces give entrepreneurial companies the traditional workplace benefits without having to front the operational expenses.

Different from coworking spaces, the Ballou Wright building on 12th Avenue offers separate office leases for businesses looking for a more traditional workplace. Jill Cronauer, president of Hunters Capital, which owns and manages the Ballou Wright building, said that these spaces are becoming the cost-effective option for small teams.

“There’s a huge distinction about small office space that’s super critical because it’s more affordable,” Cronauer said. “It’s also acting as an essential step down if an organization is resizing and downsizing.”

Cronauer also highlighted the importance of Capitol Hill’s creative atmosphere and access to mass transit as attractive features for businesses. The Ballou Wright building houses many independent tenants, such as marketers, interior designers and architecture firms.

Liz Dunn , developer of The Cloud Room and Chophouse Row , said the coworking space has become a launching pad for many independent businesses, some of which she said eventually grow beyond what the space can provide.

“We always have noticed and love the fact that we have been able to incubate little companies that have then gone on to grow,” Dunn said. “Sometimes we are able to incubate a Cloud Room member company into a user of a different office space at Chophouse. It gives us enormous satisfaction to play that role.”

Locally, shared workspaces have served as launchpads for Seattle’s startups and small businesses. On Capitol Hill, food and drink entrepreneur Makini Howell moved her administrative team into The Cloud Room, where she collaborated with fellow tenant and graphic design studio Wildern on the brand’s identity. Meanwhile, spaces like Foundations on Boylston and CENTRL Office on 11th host dozens of early-stage technical founders. Across the city, coworking hubs and incubators including The Pioneer Collective, 9Zero, AI House , and Waterfront Workspaces have helped launch notable local ventures ranging from screen-free kids’ phone maker Tin Can and proptech startup YIMBY AI to applied-AI companies Lexion, Yoodli, and Vercept .

Some of these offices offer amenities like large meeting rooms, private phone booths, Wi-Fi and coffee in their memberships, which cuts a lot of the overhead costs associated with a traditional office building.
For larger employers, taking on traditional commercial leases and custom tenant improvements remains standard practice.

Pittsburgh-based Duolingo, which employs roughly 900 people globally and operates a regional engineering and product outpost of a few dozen staffers in Capitol Hill, signed a lease in 2024 for 7,940 square feet of office space inside the six-story Bullitt Center. Leasing an entire floorplate in one of the neighborhood’s signature commercial buildings gives the publicly traded edtech company room to customize its own workspace — while underscoring the gap between institutional tech tenants and the solo founders or small teams turning to shared spaces to avoid buildout costs.
In addition to providing independent businesses support, Dunn also said that office space plays an important role for the economy and the identity of the neighborhood.
“A truly successful 24/7 neighborhood has to have residents, retail, and office,” Dunn said. “And I wish we had more office space on Capitol Hill than we do.”

articles.title: Seattle launches community process to rename Jackson Park — Jackson Street? Not yet
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: Mayor Katie Wilson has directed Seattle Parks and Recreation to launch a public process to rename north Seattle’s Jackson Park , responding to what she says are community calls for a title that better reflects the land’s history and the city’s values.

Originally named after President Andrew Jackson whose policies forcibly displaced Native American peoples, the park at 1000 NE 135th has faced scrutiny from residents questioning the legacy. The renaming initiative coincides with new light rail service and planned pedestrian and bicycle upgrades designed to improve neighborhood access to the park and its golf course.
“With new light rail connections and opportunities to make the park more accessible and welcoming, we should have a park that reflects the values of our city,” Wilson said.
Groups have also pushed for better community use of the park, including tough questions about the future of the golf course and potential for future affordable housing development.
Under the City’s Park Naming Policy, SPR is inviting residents to submit name proposals by Monday, December 14th.

The parks naming committee will evaluate suggestions based on the land’s history, natural features, geographical location, and cultural significance, including Indigenous ties to the area. Proposals may also honor a community contributor deceased for at least three years. Written submissions, including a brief rationale, can be sent via email to PKS_BPRC@seattle.gov. The committee will review the entries and recommend a final choice to the department superintendent.
The debate over Jackson Park also draws attention to Seattle’s other prominent Andrew Jackson namesake: South Jackson Street.

The major thoroughfare through Pioneer Square, the Chinatown–International District, and the Central District was platted by city co-founder David “Doc” Maynard in 1853. While periodic community proposals have called for renaming the street—or symbolically rededicating it to a different figure without changing addresses , similar to how King County was rededicated from Vice President William Rufus King to Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. —any formal street name change requires a Seattle City Council ordinance and involves significant logistical hurdles for affected residents, businesses, and transit agencies.

Jackson is far from the only Seattle landmark with a contested history; Maynard’s original 1853 street grid also honored pro-slavery and secessionist politicians on neighboring South King Street (William Rufus King) and South Lane Street (Joseph Lane), while other city streets and parks commemorate slaveholders like James Madison and Thomas Jefferson, as well as territorial Governor Isaac Stevens, who coerced local Indigenous tribes into ceding their lands.
Alongside the renaming effort, SPR is gathering broader feedback on park safety, cleanliness, and trail conditions through an upcoming online survey.

articles.title: Hollingsworth celebrates $6M economic growth fund for Central District and Southeast Seattle in final budget push
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: As the full Seattle City Council prepares for one last vote finalizing the city’s 2027-2028 budget, District 3 representative and Council President Joy Hollingsworth is celebrating the inclusion of a $6 million economic growth fund she championed to power community investments in the Central District and Southeast Seattle.

Seattle’s Select Budget Committee approved the budget amendment sponsored by Hollingsworth allocating $3.2 million in 2027 and $2.8 million in 2028 to the Central District/Southeast Seattle Fund . According to Hollingsworth, the measure aims to “preserve cultural heritage and foster economic growth” across District 3 and South Seattle.
The program will serve as a “targeted reinvestment mechanism” for community-led initiatives, cultural institutions, and small businesses, Hollingsworth says.

“Supporting community organizations, small businesses and people that preserve and revitalize the Central District and southeast Seattle communities is why this fund exists,” Hollingsworth said, thanking budget chair Dan Strauss and co-sponsors Councilmembers Dionne Foster and Rob Saka .

Beginning in 2027, the Seattle Department of Neighborhoods will manage the funds via a “structured and transparent application process” supported by two full-time staff members. Department director Quynh Pham noted that local organizations play a vital role in preserving the area’s “history, culture, and sense of belonging.”

Friday’s final vote will a contentious week in which council members approved more than 100 amendments to Mayor Katie Wilson’s spending plan, which had originally been shaped to close a projected $175 million shortfall without dipping into reserves or new taxes. Council changes included a decision to raid $31 million in JumpStart payroll tax reserves to cover council amendments to Wilson’s proposal. The tax was originally shaped to fund affordable housing and services coming out of the pandemic.
The full council is expected to pass the 2027-2028 spending plan Friday but Councilmember Maritza Rivera said she will not vote for the budget.

“I cannot in good conscience recommend this budget. It is not fiscally responsible or sustainable,” Rivera said in a statement. “This budget continues the bad habit of adding without balancing and relying, in part, on JumpStart reserves to cover those adds. This undoes our previous commitment to rebuild the JumpStart reserves. It is simply bad budgeting.”
The full City Council will vote on the final 2027-2028 budget Friday at 1 PM before sending it to the mayor for signature.

articles.title: The Black Futures Book Club at LANGSTON Takes Readers on a Journey to Other Worlds
paras: Every month this year, members of LANGSTON's Black Futures Book Club discussed literary works where afrofuturism played a core theme. With two meetings left before the year ends, facilitator Dr. Brooke Bosley is preparing for the 2027 curriculum, confirming that the Black Futures Book Club will have a future at LANGSTON.

"When you traditionally think of science fiction, you think about Octavia E. Butler, and that may be it for a lot of people," said Bosley. "During these past few years, we've been able to introduce people to so many different writers and subspaces that we might have never thought about picking up, like speculative writing."

The Black Futures Book Club meets every fourth Monday, from 6 to 7:30 p.m. Events are free and vary from in-person to virtual gatherings. The last two meetings of the year will be held virtually to accommodate the upcoming holidays. At the club's next meeting on Nov. 23, readers will discuss Son of the Morning by Akwaeke Emezi. On Dec. 28, the book under discussion will be Ring Shout by P. Djeli Clark.

This year's afrofuturism theme took readers on a journey through time, inviting them to engage with literature that either uses time to challenge and reimagine society or requires readers to look to the future for solutions to today's problems. Some recent works include We Are the Crisis by Cadwell Turnbull; When the Reckoning Comes by LaTanya McQueen; and The Black Girl Survives in This One: Horror Stories , an anthology.
Bosley's favorite works were speculative fiction, a genre that morphs the narrative setting from a pragmatic reality into a fantastical, supernatural, futuristic, or alternative hypothetical world.

" As the Earth Dreams: Black Canadian Speculative Stories was really good," said Bosley. "Even though they were short stories, they were so beautifully written. Each one had me thinking about the speculative story differently, and it introduced me to a whole new subset [of literature]."

Bosley says that next year, the primary goal of the book club will be to have fun. "We're gonna be reading stories about reimagining Black joy," said Bosley. "We're trying to do more author talks, more activities, and really just have fun with reading."
Bosley started the Black Futures Book Club about three years ago alongside Kristina Clark, who ran LOVING ROOM: diaspora books + salon in the Central District at the time.
"We began to talk about wanting a space where we could read science fiction [and] Black future stories, and imagine something different. But it also came out of self-interest," Bosley said.

Bosley, who moved to Seattle in 2022 after getting a job as a researcher at Microsoft, is a Black feminist scholar. According to her website, her scholarship work stands at the intersection of afrofuturism, Black feminism, human-computer interaction, and race and technology, and is meant to "challenge and reimagine conventional design principles and practices that are often grounded by colonialism." Bosley has a doctorate and a Master of Science in digital media from the Georgia Institute of Technology.
The Black Futures Book Club is a multigenerational space, and Bosley says one of her favorite parts of facilitating the club is seeing people of all ages coming together to enjoy reading.

"Someone from the club reached out to me earlier this year and said, 'Thank you so much for providing a space where older Black women can be seen and have a space to talk and do things, because I'm learning about myself,'" said Bosley. "And that is a really nice part of it: that everyone comes with a different variety and walk of life."

articles.title: Immigration enforcement continues to impact local families
articles.author: Jaelynn Grisso
paras: Six-year-old Victoria went to downtown Seattle earlier this year after being called in for an immigration court hearing. Officials had marked her as an “unaccompanied minor” - despite the fact she came to the U.S. with her parents - and separated her case from her parents’ case.
Advocates working closely with families told Cascade PBS they frequently see this process of separating kids' cases from their parents and believe it’s a tactic to sow confusion.

“In the last year we've really seen an escalation in the attacks by ICE on migrant families, migrant children, migrant women," said Anna Beyette, an organizer with International Women’s Alliance. “What we've actually seen, since the start of the year, is the escalation of particularly children's courts into something that they're referring to as ‘mega master’ hearings.”

Those hearings often saw dockets with a hundred cases or more per day. Beyette says the mega master hearings have slowed since this summer, but the number of cases in a regular court day has still gone up. She estimates that dockets had about a dozen cases a day before the mega master hearings began, and now they have an average of 50 60 cases in a regular court day.

In the first half of this year, more than 300 children were arrested as part of immigration enforcement in Washington. But that is only a fraction of the kids who have ongoing cases and could be called into court. Beyette estimates the number of children with hearings this year to be over a thousand.

“It's terrifying for the children. Many of them are young,” Beyette said. “When you go in there, you see families with babies and toddlers who are there for their toddlers' appointments. And so to ask children to advocate for themselves oftentimes in like not their native language, without proper information to them about what's happening, is just really a violation of their human rights.”
Many of those arrested are between 10 and 14 years old. But some arrests are for kids much younger, including a handful that were under a year old.

As for 6-year-old Victoria, Beyette and many others successfully rallied to push for her case to be reconnected to her mom’s case. She says she sees that as a win not just for Victoria, but for every family encountering this situation.

“One thing that I really want to make very clear is that even as there are these heightened attacks on migrant families and our communities, we're seeing people fighting back,” she said. “Even as they're afraid for their families, they're fighting back because migrants always are at the forefront of fighting not just for their families, but to end a system that is forcing them from their homelands and then targeting them when they come here to the U.S.”
Home Depot parking lots were once a place for those looking for a day’s work to gather.
During late summer and early fall, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents were responsible for a surge in arrests of day laborers at Seattle-area home improvement big box stores.
In the months since, those crackdowns have reportedly decreased in the Seattle area.
KUOW reporter Gustavo Sagrero Álvarez has been covering immigration enforcement surges at Seattle metro-area Home Depots.

Sagrero Álvarez said what's often not talked about is that the men searching for work span the spectrum of immigration status, including U.S. citizens, asylum seekers, and likely a significant number without legal status.

“One of the gentlemen that I spoke to in the story, he had been here [in Washington] for two years recently, and his family was back in Mexico, and he was here living in the United States - working in the United States without documentation,” said Gustavo Sagrero Álvarez, who covers the intersection of race and identity.

“And he was trying to figure out how to maintain his life here, sustain himself, while also sending what he could back to his family. There are other people, though, that have been here for so much longer. Decades, you know, sometimes even longer than I've been alive. Which is kind of crazy to think, you know, at least for somebody who's 30 years old, right? And these gentlemen have been making a living doing this kind of workday, in and day out for, for that long,” Sagrero Álvarez said.

Since those surges, people looking for work in those parking lots, are often few and far between in the Seattle metro area. However, east of Seattle in Central Washington, Sagrero Alvarez noted similar surges are happening in Yakima, an area with a large Latino population.

The Department of Homeland Security said it has no plans to stop deportations. The agency said in a statement: “ICE is NOT backing away or slowing down. Under the leadership of President Trump and Secretary Mullin, DHS will continue to enforce our nation’s laws and remove criminal illegal aliens from our streets.”
Meanwhile, Sagrero Álvarez says many of the men arrested by ICE agents are in varying situations.

“Some folks are still fighting their cases to stay in the United States. It's a mix of people are in the immigrant lockup in Tacoma, and then others have already been deported out,” he said. “And there are in some cases, I haven't heard yet of anybody being released back into the community just yet. But that would be that would be the next story.”
Will the “blue wave” in Congress bring about the change voters expressed they wanted at the ballot box?
On January 3rd, the 120 th Congress will be sworn in with Democrats in the majority in both the U.S. House and Senate.
Washington Rep. Adam Smith, who won re-election in the state’s Congressional 9 th District, says getting things done will be difficult as the President has said he’ll use his veto power.

But Smith says his party will prioritize passing legislation that helps the American people and addresses corruption. “Fixing immigration policy, getting after the tariffs, getting after the health care issues -policies that reverse the very damaging policies that the Trump administration has put in place. And then second, going after the corruption. Holding the Trump administration responsible for just all the illegal activity that they've done, some of that is just directly enriching the President and his friends.” Rep. Smith said.
Smith says immigration enforcement today is “an abomination” under the Trump administration.

He says he doesn’t support open borders but believes there is a legitimate policy difference between open borders, and what he calls the administration’s draconian crackdown. He says those policies have created “a campaign of terror” on immigrant populations.

Washington state houses one of the nation’s private immigration detection centers, the Northwest ICE Processing Center in Tacoma. It has seen a significant increase in its population size under the Trump administration and heavy scrutiny for reported human rights violations. Cascade PBS has reported on a series of those complaints inside the facility, from what happens when there is an assault in the Northwest ICE Detention Center, to concerns over legal service access , and on i nvestigations into how immigrant rights groups mobilize as the federal government pushes for deportation.
Smith says immigration detention centers face fewer regulations and requirements than federal prisons.

“I think we need to get rid of private prisons. (Rep.) Pramila Jayapal and I have had, for a decade now, a bill to reform that, to get rid of private prisons and put in place standards and requirements for these detention facilities.” Smith said.
Meanwhile, post the midterms, in a 60 Minutes interview that aired on CBS the President admitted his “deportation policy was too tough.”

“The President says stuff. It doesn’t - doesn't mean anything. I mean, he says that and then he makes Stephen Miller his Chief, his Chief of Staff. And, you know, I see no evidence that Trump is going to reverse those policies,” Smith said.
When her son was a junior at Seattle’s Franklin High School, Shannon Underwood offered his school something most parents can’t: her expertise as an immigration attorney.
It led her to a legal clinic there, where she sat down with immigrant families answering a hard question: Who would care for their children if they were detained or deported?
“Every parent’s number one concern is what happens if I’m arrested and my child’s left behind,” she said. “There’s a lot of tears and a lot of fear in this.”

Underwood and other volunteers helped parents fill out guardianship and power-of-attorney paperwork, naming a trusted adult to step in if a family is separated. Some parents went a step further at the 2025 clinic, preparing papers that would let their children travel alone to Mexico to join them if they were deported, Underwood said.

“We were encouraging people to essentially prepare for the worst,” she said. “It was wonderful to see the community come together the way that it did — the efforts by the school to take care of their immigrant community.”

Amid a surge in immigration enforcement, attorneys, advocates and some schools across Western Washington are urging more immigrant families to make these documents, often called “immigrant safety plans.”

“It’s absolutely important,” said Lu Jiang, who manages the immigrant safety plan program at Legal Counsel for Youth and Children, a Seattle legal nonprofit. “This is a community resource. It’s a resource for everyone.”

LCYC created its plan in 2017 in response to the first Trump administration’s immigration policies, Jiang said. Today, its 46-page packet , available in 12 languages, includes a step-by-step guide along with two legal forms parents can fill out. LCYC’s version is among the best-known plans, but it’s not the only one.
“There are multiple ways to do this,” Jiang said.
